modules.title: Why evaluate at all
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the problem evaluation solves before any mechanism.
modules.summary: Without evaluation, 'the AI works' is a feeling, not a fact. This module frames the problem evals solve and the simplest useful mental model, before we open up how an eval actually runs.
objectives: Explain why subjective 'it looks good' testing fails for AI systems.
Identify the main tradeoff instead of treating the topic as trivia.
Choose one validation check that would catch a realistic failure.

spans.text: Why this exists:
you change a prompt, eyeball five outputs, and ship. Two weeks later users report the model now botches a case you never re-checked.
Evaluation
exists to replace that gut-feel spot-check with a repeatable, measured answer to 'did this change make things better or worse?'
Before reading on, predict:
if you only ever judge an AI by glancing at a few outputs, what kind of failure are you almost guaranteed to miss?

blocks.title: The core idea: a standard you can re-run

spans.text: An
eval
is just a repeatable test of an AI system's quality. Instead of judging outputs by feel, you fix a set of cases, run the system on them, and score the results the same way every time.
The mental model to carry: an eval is a
frozen standard
. Because the cases don't change, the only thing that moves the score is the system itself. That's what makes 'better or worse than last week?' an answerable question.

items.text: Eyeballing a few outputs samples whatever you happened to look at; an eval samples the same fixed cases every run.
An eval catches a
regression
— a change that quietly breaks a case that used to work — which spot-checking almost never does.
Keep one tracked score attached to the system so every change has a number, not an opinion.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the four parts of an eval

spans.text: Every
eval
, from a one-line script to a hosted platform, is the same four parts wired in a line.

items.text: Dataset
— a fixed set of
test cases
, each an input and (often) an expected answer. This is what holds your standard steady across runs.
Run
— feed each input to the AI system and collect its actual output.
Scorer
— compare each output to the expected answer (or grade it against a
rubric
) and emit pass/fail or a number.
Score
— aggregate the per-case results into one tracked metric (e.g. 86% pass) you compare across versions to catch a
regression

spans.text: The whole point of fixing the dataset is repeatability: run the same cases before and after a change and the score moves only because the system changed, not because you happened to look at different examples.

blocks.title: Minimal working eval

spans.text: All four parts from module 2 are here: the
dataset
list, the run (calling the system), the exact-match scorer, and the aggregated score. This is the smallest runnable shape; you'd swap exact-match for a rubric or judge as cases get fuzzier.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it: if my_model returns "4.0" for the first case, what pass rate prints — and why?
predictThenReveal.answer: 50%. "4.0" != "4" under exact-match, so case 1 fails even though it's arithmetically correct. This is exactly why exact-match is brittle and you sometimes reach for a rubric or judge.

syntax.explains: Aggregates per-case results into one score.

spans.text: Verify the AI-generated version before trusting it.
If you have an assistant write an eval harness, check these four things specific to evals:

items.text: Is the scorer comparing the right fields? A harness that scores output against output (not against
expected
) will report 100% and prove nothing.
Does it normalize before comparing (whitespace, case)? Otherwise correct answers fail on formatting, as in the prediction above.
Is the dataset fixed and version-controlled? If cases are generated fresh each run, the score is not comparable across versions.
Does it report per-case failures, not just the aggregate? A bare pass rate hides which inputs broke.

modules.title: Trust, check, and ship
modules.sub: Late step: where evals mislead, then lock it in with recall.
modules.summary: An eval can pass and still lie to you. This module covers how evals break in practice, recalls the four parts from module 2 to make them stick, and ends with a decision checklist for shipping.
objectives: Name two ways a passing eval can still be misleading.
Identify the main tradeoff instead of treating the topic as trivia.
Choose one validation check that would catch a realistic failure.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict from memory:
back in module 2 you saw an eval has four moving parts. Can you name all four in order before scrolling?
The four parts were:
dataset
(fixed test cases), run (collect outputs), scorer (grade them), and score (the aggregate you track). The failure modes below are each a way one of those four parts quietly betrays you.
A green pass rate feels like proof. These are the ways it can be lying to you — each one maps to a part of the eval.

items.text: Overfitting the dataset.
You tune prompts until the
dataset
passes, so the score measures memorization of those cases, not real-world quality. Hold out a fresh set you never tune against.
Judge bias.
An
LLM-as-judge
systematically prefers longer or more confident answers, inflating scores for verbose-but-wrong outputs. Spot-check judge verdicts against human labels.
Silent regressions outside the dataset.
The eval only covers what's in it; a
regression
on an untested case is invisible. When a real bug slips through, add it as a new case so it can never regress unnoticed again.
Metric mismatch.
Exact-match counts a correct answer as a failure over formatting, so the score drops for the wrong reason and you 'fix' a problem that wasn't there.

questions.q: What decision does AI Evaluation Foundations change in your build?
questions.why: A lesson is useful only when it changes what you do next.

spans.text: Reconstruct the lesson from memory before reading on:

(1) Why do evals exist instead of eyeballing outputs? (2) What are the four moving parts of an eval? (3) Name the three scoring methods and their main tradeoff. (4) What's the smallest runnable eval shape? (5) Name two ways a passing eval can still mislead you.
If any answer was fuzzy, that's the module to reopen. The through-line: an
eval
turns 'it seems to work' into a fixed dataset, a repeatable run, an explicit scorer, and a tracked score you can compare across versions.

capstone.prompt: Solo build: take a small AI feature you have (or a prompt) and write a runnable eval for it from scratch — a fixed dataset of 5+ cases, a run that collects outputs, a scorer (start with exact-match), and a printed aggregate score. Then add one holdout case the system currently fails. NEXT RUNG: once you trust the score, replace exact-match with an LLM-as-judge and validate it against your own labels on 10 cases — that's the gateway to the 'LLM-as-judge calibration' lesson.
